TO: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services FILE CODE: CMS-0062-P FEDERAL REGISTER CITATION: 91 FR 19890 (April 14, 2026) DATE: April 22, 2026 FROM: Helsesoft LLC / GreenLight PA, Bellevue, Washington RE: Comment on the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs  Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P) I. Introduction and Commenter Identity Helsesoft LLC is a Washington State health technology company and the developer of  GreenLight PA, a prior authorization intelligence platform built specifically for dermatology.  GreenLight PA maintains a structured, machine-readable library of prior authorization (PA)  criteria for dermatology biologics — including agents such as dupilumab, tralokinumab,  risankizumab, and secukinumab — mapped at the drug, insurer, and state level across major  commercial payers including Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans,  and commercial QHP issuers. The platform is EHR-independent and contains no protected  health information (PHI) by architectural design, enabling deployment across practice settings of  all sizes. Helsesoft LLC was founded by a physician with direct experience in healthcare workflow design  and clinical operations, and has built GreenLight PA in close collaboration with practicing  dermatologists. The company’s development work has required sustained, direct engagement  with payer coverage policy documents across multiple drug-indication combinations, insurers,  and states — giving us ground-level technical understanding of how prior authorization criteria  are published, structured, updated, and applied in practice. This comment reflects that  operational experience. We strongly support CMS’s proposal to extend prior authorization interoperability requirements  to drugs. The sections below address specific provisions of the proposed rule and respond to  two of CMS’s explicit Requests for Information. II. Support for Extending Electronic PA Requirements to Drugs Relevant sections: II.B (Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs); II.C (Improving  Communications and Decision Timeframes); 91 FR 19890 The 2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F) made meaningful  progress on non-drug PA but created an anomalous gap for specialties like dermatology where  virtually all high-cost, high-efficacy treatments are biologics dispensed under pharmacy or  medical benefits. For a dermatology practice, the practical effect of CMS-0057-F was limited:  the most burdensome authorization workflows — for drugs like dupilumab, which routinely  requires multi-step documentation of prior treatment failure across multiple insurers — remained  entirely outside its scope. CMS-0062-P closes that gap. We specifically support the following proposed provisions: •Section II.B.3: Incorporating drugs covered under a medical benefit into the Prior  Authorization API for all impacted payers. Biologics for dermatologic conditions are  frequently billed under the medical benefit (Part B for Medicare Advantage), making this  provision essential for dermatology. •Section II.B.5: Requiring support for the NCPDP Formulary and Benefit Standard, which  will enable providers and their health IT tools to query formulary information and real- time coverage status for covered drugs. •Section II.C.2: Requiring a specific reason for denial in response to PA requests for all  drugs. In our experience maintaining payer policy documentation for dermatology  biologics, denial reasons as currently communicated are frequently generic and  insufficient to guide resubmission. •Section II.C.3: Proposed shorter decision timeframes aligned across MA, Medicaid,  CHIP, and QHP programs. Standardizing timeframes across program types significantly  reduces administrative complexity for practices managing patients across payer types. •Section II.C.7: Requiring public reporting of PA metrics for drugs. This is the  transparency foundation on which downstream accountability mechanisms can be built. III. A Critical Gap: Published Criteria vs. Real-World Approval Behavior Relevant sections: II.C.7 (Public Reporting of Drug PA Metrics); III.D (Request for Information:  Step Therapy); 91 FR 19890 We write to draw CMS’s attention to a structural problem in the prior authorization ecosystem  that the proposed rule’s transparency provisions begin to address but do not fully reach: the  divergence between payers’ published prior authorization criteria and the criteria actually  applied in approval and denial decisions. In maintaining GreenLight PA’s structured policy library — which monitors coverage policy  documents for dermatology biologics across more than 200 drug-insurer-state combinations —  we have observed systematic patterns in which published payer criteria do not reliably predict  actual approval behavior. These patterns include: • Step therapy sequences documented in published coverage policies that are  inconsistently enforced in practice, with some insurers approving requests that bypass  stated requirements while denying others that appear to satisfy them. • Documentation standards described in policy language that differ materially from what is  actually required for approval as reflected in denial rationale communications. • Coverage criteria that are updated in practice — through apparent internal guidance —  without corresponding updates to published policy documents, creating a lag during  which providers and their tools are operating on outdated information. These patterns create measurable harm. Providers build PA submissions around published  criteria that may not reflect what the insurer actually requires, leading to avoidable denials,  resubmission cycles, and delays in patient access to therapy. The public reporting requirements  in Section II.C.7 represent important progress, but aggregate approval and denial rate metrics  do not directly surface whether payers are applying their own stated criteria consistently. IV. Specific Recommendations A. Require Drug-Level and Specialty-Level Granularity in Public PA Metrics Relevant section: II.C.7 (Proposed Requirement To Publicly Report Prior Authorization Metrics  for Drugs); 91 FR 19890 We recommend that CMS require impacted payers to report PA approval and denial metrics  disaggregated by therapeutic area or clinical specialty (e.g., dermatology, rheumatology,  oncology) in addition to the proposed drug-level reporting. Dermatology biologics carry  authorization burden profiles substantially different from other drug categories: they are typically  chronic therapies, require documentation of prior treatment failure, and involve step therapy  sequences that vary significantly by insurer and state. Aggregate drug-level metrics will obscure  this variation. Specialty-level disaggregation would enable CMS, researchers, provider organizations, and the  public to identify areas of disproportionate burden and target oversight accordingly. It would also  allow specialty societies to monitor payer performance within their domain — a form of  distributed accountability that requires no additional CMS enforcement infrastructure. B. Require Payers to Publish Machine-Readable, Structured PA Criteria for Covered  Drugs Relevant sections: II.A.4(a)(6) (Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS Implementation Guides); II.B.3  (Prior Authorization API for Drugs Under Medical Benefit); 91 FR 19890 CMS-0062-P requires payers to implement electronic PA APIs enabling providers to submit  requests and receive decisions electronically. We strongly support this. However, the ability to  submit a PA request electronically does not, by itself, ensure that providers understand what the  payer requires for approval. The underlying PA criteria — step therapy requirements, diagnostic  thresholds, prior treatment history requirements, quantity limits, and documentation standards  — remain largely inaccessible in structured, machine-readable form. The Da Vinci Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD) and Documentation Templates and  Rules (DTR) implementation guides identified in Section II.A.4(a)(6) represent the right technical  direction: they are designed to surface coverage requirements to providers at the point of care.  We recommend that CMS strengthen the proposed rule by requiring impacted payers to  implement CRD and DTR as mandatory — not merely recommended — components of the  Prior Authorization API for drugs. This would: • Enable providers and health IT tools to surface accurate, payer-specific requirements at  the point of care, reducing avoidable denials driven by documentation gaps. • Create an auditable, structured record of the criteria payers have committed to applying,  against which actual decisions can be evaluated. • Reduce duplicative manual research burden on practices that currently must interpret  narrative PDF policy documents across multiple payers to determine what is required for  a given drug. We acknowledge that payers may seek to protect commercially sensitive aspects of their  coverage criteria. We do not propose disclosure of proprietary adjudication logic or internal risk  models. We propose only that the criteria a treating provider must satisfy to obtain approval be  made available in structured, queryable form via the APIs CMS is already requiring payers to  build. C. Response to RFI III.D: Step Therapy Relevant section: III.D (Request for Information: Step Therapy); 91 FR 19890 CMS’s request for information on step therapy (Section III.D) directly implicates the divergence  problem described in Section III of this comment. Step therapy is the single most consequential  structural feature of drug PA criteria for dermatology biologics, and it is also the area where the  gap between published criteria and applied criteria is most pronounced and most harmful. In our operational experience monitoring payer policy documentation for dermatology biologics,  step therapy requirements are the most frequently updated, most inconsistently enforced, and  most difficult to interpret elements of published coverage criteria. We offer the following  observations in response to CMS’s request: •Step therapy requirements vary materially across payers and states for the same  drug. A provider prescribing dupilumab for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis may  face step therapy requirements ranging from one prior topical agent to multiple systemic  agents depending on the insurer and the patient’s state. Published criteria for the same  drug can require meaningfully different prior treatment histories across payers, creating  significant administrative burden for practices managing diverse patient populations. •Published step therapy criteria are frequently inconsistent with actual approval  behavior. We have observed patterns where payers appear to approve requests that do  not satisfy stated step therapy sequences, and deny requests that do — suggesting that  internal adjudication guidance diverges from published coverage policy. This divergence  is opaque to providers and impossible to anticipate from published documents alone. •The proposed metrics reporting requirements do not capture step therapy  compliance. Aggregate approval and denial rates do not reveal whether denials are  based on the step therapy requirements documented in published policy, unstated  internal criteria, or administrative deficiencies in submission. CMS should consider  requiring payers to report denial reasons at a level of granularity that includes the  specific criterion cited — including whether step therapy requirements were the basis for  denial. We recommend that CMS use the step therapy RFI to explore requiring payers to: (1) publish  step therapy requirements for covered drugs in structured, machine-readable form; (2) include  step therapy criterion citation in denial reason communications; and (3) attest annually that  published step therapy requirements reflect criteria actually applied during the reporting period.  These measures would address the root cause of much of the PA burden that this proposed  rule aims to reduce. D. Response to RFI III.C: Improving Implementation of Payer API Technology Relevant section: III.C (Request for Information: Improving Implementation of Payer API  Technology); 91 FR 19890 CMS’s request for information on improving payer API implementation (Section III.C) raises  questions directly relevant to our experience as a health IT developer serving specialty  practices. We offer the following observations: •EHR-independent middleware tools are essential for broad provider adoption. The  electronic PA API framework proposed in CMS-0062-P is designed to enable exchange  between payers and providers or their EHR systems. In practice, many specialty  practices — particularly independent dermatology practices, which represent a  substantial share of the prescribers of dermatology biologics — operate with EHR  systems that have limited or delayed PA API integration. EHR-independent health IT  tools that can consume payer APIs and surface PA requirements at the point of care are  a critical link in the adoption chain. CMS’s implementation guidance should explicitly  acknowledge and support this model. •API standardization does not eliminate the need for policy intelligence tools. Even  with standardized FHIR APIs in place, providers will need tools to interpret coverage  requirements, compare drug options across payers, and guide PA submission content.  The intelligence layer — translating structured payer data into actionable clinical  guidance — remains a product and workflow challenge that the API framework alone  does not resolve. CMS should consider this when evaluating whether the proposed  technical requirements are sufficient to achieve the rule’s burden-reduction goals. •API endpoint publication (Section II.E) will meaningfully improve the developer  ecosystem. The proposed requirement for payers to report and CMS to publish API  endpoint information (Section II.E) is a practical improvement that will reduce the  discovery burden for health IT developers building tools that consume payer APIs. We  support this provision and recommend that CMS require endpoint publication to include  API version information and conformance testing results to enable developers to assess  compatibility without direct payer engagement. V. Conclusion Helsesoft LLC and GreenLight PA strongly support CMS-0062-P’s extension of electronic prior  authorization and transparency requirements to drugs. The proposed rule addresses a genuine  gap in the regulatory framework established by CMS-0057-F and has the potential to  meaningfully reduce PA burden for patients awaiting access to dermatology biologics and other  specialty medications. We urge CMS to strengthen the rule by: making the CRD and DTR implementation guides  mandatory for drug PA; requiring specialty-level granularity in public metrics reporting; and  using the step therapy and API implementation RFIs to develop requirements that address the  divergence between published PA criteria and real-world approval behavior. These additions  would substantially enhance the rule’s impact and create lasting accountability in the drug PA  ecosystem. Helsesoft LLC welcomes the opportunity to provide additional technical input to CMS on any of  the issues raised in this comment. We are available for follow-up at the contact information  below.
